summary: This informational document sets out test and evaluation methods for physical network equipment in the data center. It builds on the terminology in RFC 8238, which is a prerequisite, and describes how to measure things like switch performance in a repeatable way.

plainLanguage.summary: A data centre switch has many fast ports and very little memory for buffering. This document describes how to put one on a test bench and measure the things that matter there: how fast it forwards, how much it can hold when traffic piles up, how large a burst it survives, and whether one busy port can slow down an unrelated one.

questions: how to benchmark data center switches
how to measure switch buffer size
how to test head of line blocking
subtitle: How to measure the switches in a data centre, where short bursts and tiny buffers decide how well the network behaves.

tldr.problem: The standard benchmarking methods for network devices measure theoretical throughput and latency under laboratory conditions, and they do not reproduce the traffic patterns of a data centre, where many flows of different sizes share one switch at once.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds five tests for the data centre case: line-rate forwarding, buffer measurement, microburst capacity, head-of-line blocking and an incast test that mixes TCP and UDP flows.
tldr.outcome: The result is a repeatable procedure with a fixed reporting format for each test, so that two switches can be compared on the same numbers rather than on the vendor's own claims.

sections.title: Why Data Center Gear Needs Its Own Tests
sections.content:
Traffic patterns in the data centre are not uniform and are constantly changing. They are dictated by the nature and variety of applications used there. They can be largely east-west flows, server to server inside the data centre, in one data centre, and north-south, from the outside of the data centre to the server, in another, while others may combine both. Traffic patterns can be bursty in nature and contain many-to-one, many-to-many or one-to-many flows. Each flow may also be small and latency sensitive or large and throughput sensitive, while containing a mix of UDP and TCP traffic, and all of these can coexist in a single cluster and flow through a single network device simultaneously.

Benchmarking tests for network devices have long used RFC 1242, RFC 2432, RFC 2544, RFC 2889 and RFC 3918, which have largely focused on the latency attributes and the throughput of the device being benchmarked. Those standards are good at measuring theoretical throughput, forwarding rates and latency under testing conditions, but they do not represent the real traffic patterns that may affect these devices.

Typical data centre networking devices are characterised by high port density, 48 ports or more; high speed, currently up to 100 GB/s per port; high throughput, line rate on all ports for Layer 2 and/or Layer 3; low latency, in the microsecond or nanosecond range; a low amount of buffer, in the MB range per networking device; and Layer 2 and Layer 3 forwarding capability, with Layer 3 not mandatory.

Every test in the document is written in the same three-part format: the objective, the methodology and the reporting format. For each test it is critical that repeatability of the results be obtained, so enough iterations of the given test should be performed and the result checked for consistency. This is especially important for the buffering test, which has historically been the least reliable. The number of iterations should be explicitly reported, and the relative standard deviation should be below 10 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing benchmark methods answer the wrong question for a data centre. They ask how fast a port can go on its own. A data centre switch has to hold dozens of ports at full speed at once, with only a few megabytes of memory to absorb the moment when they do not quite match up, so the tests have to look at those moments instead.

sections.title: Line-Rate Testing and the Snake Test
sections.content:
The line-rate test is a maximum-rate test for throughput, latency and jitter, intended to verify that the device under test is capable of forwarding packets at line rate under non-congested conditions.

A traffic generator should be connected to all ports on the device, and two tests must be conducted: a port-pair test, and a test using a full-mesh device. For all tests, the traffic generator's sending rate must be less than or equal to 99.98 percent of the nominal value of the line rate, with no further parts-per-million adjustment to account for interface clock tolerances, so that the device is stressed in reasonable worst-case conditions. Test results at a lower rate may be provided for better understanding of the performance increase in latency and jitter when the rate is lower than 99.98 percent, and the receiving rate should be captured during the test as a percentage of line rate. The test must provide the statistics of minimum, average and maximum of the latency distribution, and of the jitter distribution, for the exact same iteration of the test.

When a traffic generator cannot be connected to all ports, a snake test must be used for line-rate testing, excluding latency and jitter because those become irrelevant. The first and last port of the device are connected to a traffic generator, all the ports in between are connected back to back and sequentially, port 2 to port 3, port 4 to port 5 and so on up to port N-2 to port N-1, and port 1 and port 2 are configured in the same VLAN, port 3 and port 4 in the next, and so on. This gives line-rate coverage for Layer 2 and Layer 3 with a two-port generator.

The report must include the physical-layer calibration information defined in the data centre benchmarking terminology document, the number of ports used, and the reading for throughput received as a percentage of bandwidth while sending 99.98 percent of the nominal line rate on each port, for each packet size from 64 bytes to 9216 bytes. A packet-size increment of 64 bytes between iterations is ideal, and 256-byte and 512-byte packets are also often used; the most common ordering in a report is 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1518, 4096, 8000 and 9216 bytes. Throughput is expressed as a percentage of total transmitted frames, packet drops as a count and, where possible, as a percentage of line rate, and latency and jitter in units of time, usually microseconds or nanoseconds, with minimum, average and maximum values. A histogram of the measured population is recommended for jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: The first test asks a simple question: can the switch pass traffic at the full speed of every port at once? The answer has to be given per packet size, because small packets and large packets behave differently. If you only have a traffic generator with two ports, the ports are wired up in a chain, the snake test, so that a single pair of ports can push the whole device to its limit.

sections.title: Measuring the Buffer
sections.content:
The buffering test measures the size of the buffer of a device under typical, many or multiple conditions. Buffer architectures between multiple devices can differ and include egress buffering, shared egress buffering on a switch-on-chip, ingress buffering or a combination, and the methodology covers the measurement regardless of the architecture used.

The method is based on using known congestion of known fixed packet size along with maximum latency measurements. The maximum latency increases until the first packet drop occurs, and at that point it remains constant, which is the inflection point. There must be multiple ingress ports receiving a known amount of frames at a known fixed size, destined for the same egress port, in order to create a known congestion condition. The total amount of packets sent from the oversubscribed port minus one, multiplied by the packet size, represents the maximum port buffer size at that inflection point.

Four procedures follow. The first measures the highest buffer efficiency: the packet size is varied, starting at 64 bytes, while another port sends a low amount of oversubscription traffic, 1 percent recommended, of the same size to the same egress port, and the buffer size is measured at each step; the size that yields the largest buffer is the one that allows the highest buffer efficiency. The second procedure measures the maximum port buffer size at that fixed packet size, with a fixed DSCP and class of service value of zero and for unicast traffic, by sending line rate from one ingress port to an egress port while another port oversubscribes it. The third procedure measures the maximum port pair buffer sizes, with several ingress ports sending line rate to their own egress ports while the last two ports oversubscribe other egress ports. The fourth procedure measures the maximum device buffer size with many-to-one ports, where ingress ports 1 to N-1 each send their share of the line rate to egress port N, then the roles are shifted in each iteration.

Each series may be repeated with the different class of service values of traffic and then with multicast traffic, in order to find out whether there is any impact on the buffer size. Unicast traffic, and then multicast traffic, should be used in order to determine the proportion of buffer for the documented selection of tests, and the class of service value for the packets should be provided for each test iteration, as the buffer allocation size may differ per class of service value. It is recommended that the ingress and egress ports be varied in a random but documented fashion over multiple tests, in order to measure the buffer size for each port of the device.
sections.plainLanguage: To find out how much the switch can hold, the test deliberately tips one output port over capacity with a second input and watches the delay. The delay climbs while the queue grows, then stops climbing at the moment the first packet is dropped, and the amount queued at that point is the size of the buffer. The same measurement is then made for single ports, for pairs, and for the whole device.

sections.title: Microbursts and Head-of-Line Blocking
sections.content:
The microburst test finds the maximum amount of packet bursts that a device can sustain under various configurations. All bursts should be sent with 100 percent intensity, and all ports of the device must be used for the test, with it recommended that all ports be tested simultaneously.

A traffic generator must be connected to all ports on the device. To cause congestion, two or more ingress ports must send bursts of packets destined for the same egress port, and the simplest setup is two ingress ports and one egress port. The burst is sent with an intensity of 100 percent, meaning that the burst of packets is sent with a minimum inter-packet gap. The number of packets in the burst is the trial variable and increases until there is a non-zero packet loss, and the aggregate number of packets from all the senders gives the maximum microburst the device can sustain. It is recommended that the ingress and egress ports be varied over multiple tests, that the intensity of the microburst be varied to obtain the capacity at various ingress rates, and that all ports be tested in various configurations, for example N-1 ingress ports sending to one egress port, then N-2 ingress ports sending to two egress ports, and finally two ingress ports sending to N-2 egress ports.

Head-of-line blocking is a performance-limiting phenomenon that occurs when packets are held up by the first packet ahead, waiting to be transmitted to a different output port. The objective of the test is to understand the behaviour of the device in that scenario and measure the packet loss. Groups of four ports are used: a group has two ingress ports and two egress ports. The first ingress port must have two flows configured, each going to a different egress port, and the second ingress port congests the second egress port by sending at line rate. The goal is to measure whether there is loss on the flow towards the first egress port, which is not oversubscribed. A traffic generator must be connected to at least eight ports and should be connected using all the ports.

The differences from the RFC 2889 test are that this one starts with eight ports in two groups of four rather than four ports, that it shifts all the port numbers by one in a second iteration and continues until all ports have been first in the group, so that every permutation is tested and differences in the behaviour of the switch-on-chip are covered, and that another test expands the group of ports so that traffic is divided among four ports instead of two, at 25 percent per port rather than 50 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: A microburst is a short, violent lump of traffic arriving with no gaps at all, and it can overflow a switch even when the average rate looks fine. The test increases the lump until packets start being dropped. The head-of-line test asks a different question: if one output port is flooded, does an unrelated output port suffer? The traffic for the free port is sent alongside the flood, and any loss on it is the answer.

sections.title: Incast: Stateful and Stateless Traffic Together
sections.content:
The incast test measures the values for TCP goodput and latency with a mix of large and small flows. It is designed to simulate a mixed environment of stateful flows that require high rates of goodput and stateless flows that require low latency. Stateful flows are created by generating TCP traffic, and stateless flows using UDP traffic.

There must be multiple ingress ports receiving traffic destined for the same egress port, and there may be a mix of stateful and stateless traffic arriving on a single ingress port; the simplest setup is two ingress ports receiving traffic destined for the same egress port. One ingress port must maintain a TCP connection through the ingress port to a receiver connected to an egress port, and traffic in the TCP stream must be sent at the maximum rate allowed by the traffic generator. At the same time, the stateless traffic is sent to a receiver on the same egress port, and it must be a microburst of 100 percent intensity.

The iterations vary the number of ports in two directions. Varying the stateful traffic, the first iteration has one ingress port receiving stateful TCP traffic and one receiving stateless traffic destined for one egress port, the second has two ingress ports receiving stateful traffic and one receiving stateless traffic, and the last has N-2 ingress ports receiving stateful traffic and one receiving stateless traffic. Varying the stateless traffic, the first iteration again has one ingress port on stateful traffic and one on stateless traffic, the second has one on stateful traffic and two on stateless traffic, and the last has one on stateful traffic and N-2 on stateless traffic. The report must include the number of ingress and egress ports with the designation of stateful or stateless flow assignment, the stateful flow goodput, the stateless flow latency, and the repeatability of the test, meaning the number of iterations and the percentage of variation between results.
sections.plainLanguage: This test puts a long, greedy TCP conversation next to a short burst of UDP packets heading for the same output port. The TCP flow wants all the bandwidth, the UDP flow wants low delay, and the report gives the throughput of the first and the delay of the second, so that the two can be weighed against each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking activities as described in the document are limited to technology characterization using controlled stimuli in a laboratory environment, with dedicated address space and the constraints specified in the sections above. The benchmarking network topology is an independent test setup and must not be connected to devices that may forward the test traffic into a production network or misroute traffic to the test management network.

Benchmarking is performed on a black-box basis, relying solely on measurements observable external to the device. Special capabilities should not exist in the device specifically for benchmarking purposes, and any implications for network security arising from the device should be identical in the lab and in production networks. The document requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests run on a private network in a lab, wired so that nothing can leak into a production system. The device is measured only from the outside and must not contain special test facilities, so that what is measured in the lab is what you get in the rack.

cells: The packet size that yields the largest buffer, found by varying the size upward from 64 bytes
The buffer of each port at that packet size, with a fixed DSCP and class of service of 0, on unicast traffic

The whole device, with many ingress ports feeding a single egress port

viz.caption: MICROBURST AND HEAD-OF-LINE BLOCKING TESTS (RFC 8239, SECTIONS 4 AND 5)

items.title: Microburst
items.text: Two or more ingress ports send bursts at 100 percent intensity to the same egress port, and the burst grows until packets are lost.

items.title: Head-of-line blocking
items.text: One port sends half its traffic to each of two egress ports while another port floods the second one; the loss on the first flow is what is measured.

items.title: Shifting the ports
items.text: The test shifts the port numbers by one each iteration, so that every permutation is covered.

items.title: Wider groups
items.text: A second version splits the traffic over four egress ports instead of two, at 25 percent per port.
